# Problem 1

This problem will require you to learn things we have not covered. Use the R help, or online resources, to figure out the appropriate command(s). Use citation as necessary.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| echo: false

library(dplyr)
library(haven)
```

## a) Merge the two files to create a single data.frame. Keep only records which matched. Print out the dimensions of the merged data.frame.

```{r}

aux <- read_xpt("AUX_I.xpt")
demo <- read_xpt("DEMO_I.xpt")

data <- inner_join(aux, demo, by = "SEQN")
print(paste("The number of rows remaining is ",
            nrow(data)))
print(paste("The number of columns remaining is ",
            ncol(data)))
```

## b) We’ll be using the following variables. Clean up each - ensure all missing values are actually NA (rather than 999 or something), and if it’s categorical, convert it to factor with informative levels.

### Gender

Below, we see the meaning of the codes listed in the Gender column. 

#### 1: Male

#### 2: Female

```{r}
hist(data$RIAGENDR)
```

No Gender values are missing or lack a usual category. We therefore proceed with the data cleaned.

### Citizenship

Below, we see the meaning of the codes listed in the Citizenship column. 

#### 1: Citizen

#### 2: Not a Citizen

#### 7: Refused

#### 9: Don't Know

```{r}
print(paste("Number Refused: ",
```

## c) The Tympanometric width measure looks approximately like a Poisson distribution. Fit four Poisson regression models predicting a respondent’s Tympanometric width in each ear. Each model is defined below, for a specific ear and a specific set of covariates.

#### 1R - Right ear: gender

#### 2R - Right ear: gender, citizenship status (as categorical), number of children (as continuous), annual household income (as continuous)

#### 1L - Left ear: gender

#### 2L - Left ear: gender, citizenship status (as categorical), number of children (as continuous), annual household income (as continuous)

Produce a table presenting the estimated incidence risk ratios for the coefficients in each model, along with the sample size for the model, the pseudo-𝑅2, and AIC values. (This can be a single table, or one table for coefficients and a separate table for model statistics).

```{r}

model_1R <- glm(AUAREQC ~ RIAGENDR,
                family = poisson(link = "log"), data = data)
model_2R <- glm(AUAREQC ~ RIAGENDR
                + factor(DMDCITZN) + DMDHHSZA + INDHHIN2,
                family = poisson(link = "log"), data = data)

model_1L <- glm(AUALEQC ~ RIAGENDR,
                family = poisson(link = "log"), data = data)
model_2L <- glm(AUAREQC ~ RIAGENDR
                + factor(DMDCITZN) + DMDHHSZA + INDHHIN2,
                family = poisson(link = "log"), data = data)

```

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| echo: false

library(knitr)
library(pscl)
```

```{r}

build_metrics <- function(model) {
  c(IRR = exp(coef(model)["RIAGENDR"]),
    N   = nobs(model),
    R2  = pR2(model)["McFadden"],
    AIC = model$aic)
}


df <- data.frame(
  Model_1R = build_metrics(model_1R),
  Model_2R = build_metrics(model_2R),
  Model_1L = build_metrics(model_1L),
  Model_2L = build_metrics(model_2L)
)

df_flipped <- as.data.frame(t(df))

kable(df_flipped,
      col.names = c("Incidence Risk Ratio",
                    "Sample Size",
                    "R2",
                    "AIC"),
      digits = 3)

```

## d) From model 2L, provide evidence whether there is a difference between males and females in terms of their incidence risk ratio. Test whether the predicted value of Tympanometric width measure of the left ear differs between men and women. Include the results of the each test and their interpretation.

```{r}
summary(model_2L)
library(marginaleffects)
avg_predictions(model_2L,
                variables = "RIAGENDR")
```

We therefore conclude that males have a bigger predicted risk ratio. It is statistically significant, \[1.26, 1.37\] vs \[1.11, 1.21\].

# Problem 2 - Sakila

Use the “sakila” database discussed in class. For these problems, do not use any of the tables whose names end in list.

## a) For each store, how many customers does that store have, and what percentage of customers of that store are active in the system?

```{r}
library(DBI) 
library(dplyr)
library(microbenchmark)

db <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(),
                "sakila_master.db")

#1)

v1 <- function() {
results <- dbGetQuery(db,
                      "SELECT store_id,
                      active FROM customer")

total <- results %>%
  group_by(store_id) %>% 
  summarise(total_customers = n(),
              average_active = mean(active == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")
return(total)
}

print(v1())


#2)

v2 <- function() {
results <- dbGetQuery(db,
"SELECT store_id, AVG( CASE WHEN customer.active == 1
THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)
AS average_active,
COUNT(customer.customer_id)
AS total FROM customer GROUP BY
customer.store_id")
return(results)
}

print(v2())

microbenchmark(v1 = v1(), v2 = v2())

```

Only SQL is faster.

## b) Generate a table identifying the names and country of each staff member.

```{r}

v1 <- function() {
results <- dbGetQuery(db,
                      "SELECT * FROM staff
                      JOIN address
                      ON staff.address_id = address.address_id
                      JOIN city
                      ON city.city_id = address.city_id
                      JOIN country
                      ON city.country_id = country.country_id")
results$name <- paste(results$first_name, results$last_name)
total <- results[, c("name", "country")]
return(total)
}

print(v1())

v2 <- function() {
results <- dbGetQuery(db,
"SELECT
CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)
AS name, country
FROM staff
JOIN address
ON staff.address_id = address.address_id
JOIN city
ON city.city_id = address.city_id
JOIN country
ON city.country_id = country.country_id")
return(results)
}

print(v2())

microbenchmark(v1 = v1(), v2 = v2())

```

Only SQL is marginally faster.

## c) Identify the name(s) of the film(s) which was/were rented for the highest dollar value. (Assume all costs are in USD regardless of country.) (Hint: You can merge a table more than once.)

```{r}

v1 <- function() {
results <- dbGetQuery(db,
                      "SELECT *
                      FROM rental
                      JOIN inventory
                      ON rental.inventory_id = inventory.inventory_id
                      JOIN film
                      ON inventory.film_id = film.film_id")
results <- results[results$rental_rate == max(results$rental_rate),]
results <- unique(results$title)
return(results)
}

print("First 10:")
print(sort(v1())[1:10])

v2 <- function() {
results <- dbGetQuery(db, "SELECT
DISTINCT film.title
FROM rental
JOIN inventory
ON rental.inventory_id = inventory.inventory_id
JOIN film
ON inventory.film_id = film.film_id
WHERE film.rental_rate = (SELECT MAX(rental_rate) from film)")
return(results)
}

print("First 10:")
print(sort(head(v2()$title, 10)))

microbenchmark(v1 = v1(), v2 = v2())

```

Only SQL is faster.

# Problem 3 - Australian Records

Download the “Australia - 500 Records” data from https://www.briandunning.com/sample-data/ and import it into R. This is entirely fake data; you can read the website for details. Use it to answer the following questions.

```{r}
data <- read.csv("au-500.csv")
```

## a) What percentage of the websites are .com’s (as opposed to .net, .com.au, etc)?

```{r}
match_indices <- grep(".com$", tolower(data$web))
percent <- length(match_indices) / nrow(data)
print(paste("The percentage of the websites that are
            .com (and not .com.au) is: "
            , percent))
```

## b) What is the most common domain name amongst the email addresses? (In the email “statistics\@umich.edu”, “umich.edu” is the domain name.)

```{r}

pattern <- "@([^@]+)$"

match_rows <- regexpr(pattern, data$email, perl = TRUE)
domains <- regmatches(data$email, match_rows)

domains <- gsub("@", "", domains)
most_frequent <- names(which.max(table(domains)))
print(paste("The most frequent domain is: ",
            most_frequent))
                       
```

## c) What proportion of company names contain a non-alphabetic character, excluding commas and whitespace. (E.g. “Jane Doe, LLC” would not contain an eligible non-alphabetic character; “Plumber 247” would.) What about if you also exclude ampersands (“&”)?

```{r}
match_indices <- grep("[^a-zA-Z, ]", data$company_name)
print(paste("Proportion
            with a nonalphabetic character: ",
            length(match_indices) / nrow(data)))

match_indices <- grep("[^a-zA-Z, &]", data$company_name)
print(paste("Proportion
            with a nonalphabetic character (no ampersands): ",
            length(match_indices) / nrow(data)))
```

## d) In Australia, phone have 10 digits - but unlike in the US where we write all numbers as “123-456-7890”, they write land lines and cell phones differently. There are two different phones listed for each record. Make all phone numbers written like cell phones. Show it works by printing the first 10 phone numbers of each column.

```{r}
format_to_cell <- function(phone_col) {
  clean_digits <- gsub("\\D",
                       "", phone_col)
  gsub("(\\d{4})(\\d{3})(\\d{3})",
       "\\1-\\2-\\3",
       clean_digits)
}

data$phone1 <- format_to_cell(data$phone1)
data$phone2 <- format_to_cell(data$phone2)

head(data[, c("phone1", "phone2")], 10)
```

## e) Produce a histogram of the log of the apartment numbers for all addresses. (You may assume any number at the end of the an address is an apartment number.)

```{r}


matches <- regexec("(?i)(apt|apartment|unit|#)\\s*([a-z0-9-]+)"
                   ,data$address
                   ,perl = TRUE)

matches_list <- regmatches(data$address, matches)

apt_numbers <- sapply(matches_list,
                      function(x) if(length(x) >= 3) x[3]
                      else NA)

apt_numbers_clean <- (as.integer(na.omit(apt_numbers)))


hist(log(apt_numbers_clean),
     na.rm = TRUE)
```

## f) Benford’s law is an observation about the distribution of the leading digit of real numerical data. Examine whether the apartment numbers appear to follow Benford’s law. Do you think the apartment numbers would pass as real data?

```{r}
matches <- regexec("(?i)(apt|apartment|unit|#)\\s*([a-z0-9-]+)"
                   ,data$address
                   ,perl = TRUE)

matches_list <- regmatches(data$address, matches)

apt_numbers <- sapply(matches_list,
                      function(x) if(length(x) >= 3) x[3]
                      else NA)

apt_numbers_leading_digit <- substr(
  apt_numbers, 1, 1)

apt_numbers_leading_digit_clean <- (
  as.integer(na.omit(apt_numbers_leading_digit)))


hist(apt_numbers_leading_digit_clean,
     na.rm = TRUE)
```

Yes, we look at the histogram above and see that the lowest histogram bar is the highest bar, meaning that it has the most observations that full under it. Benford's law, also known as Newcomb–Benford law, is an observation that many real world leading digits are small. In these scenario, we see that a leading 1 is much more common than any other digit.
